table.text: Participants had a maximum of 20 minutes for 12 trials.

A headphone icon was shown on the screen while a story was playing, and participants were asked to press the keyboard space bar whenever they felt one meaningful event had ended and another event had begun.
In the first run, participants were asked to identify small events, whereas in the second run, participants were asked to identify large events in the same story.
In the main experiment, participants were asked to only identify large events.
Participants provided written informed consent prior to the experiment and were compensated $10 CAD per 30 minutes.
Data from one additional participant were recorded but excluded because of difficulties with task completion.

Participants had a maximum of 20 minutes for 12 trials.

A headphone icon was shown on the screen while a story was playing, and participants were asked to press the keyboard space bar whenever they felt one meaningful event had ended and another event had begun.
In the first run, participants were asked to identify small events, whereas in the second run, participants were asked to identify large events in the same story.
In the main experiment, participants were asked to only identify large events.
Participants provided written informed consent prior to the experiment and were compensated $10 CAD per 30 minutes.

text.text: Event segmentationthe division of continuous experience into meaningful unitsis essential for understanding narratives.
Yet little is known about how listeners segment auditory stories, how prosodic cues such as pauses contribute, and how age-related changes in hearing and cognition affect this process.
We conducted two experiments to address these questions.

In Experiment 1, human and advanced AI voices for audiobooks and podcast monologues produced longer pauses at thematic event boundaries than within events, indicating that pause timing aligns with narrative structure.
In Experiment 2, younger (19-35 years old) and older (56-79 years old) adults listened to stories in which pauses were selectively prolonged at event boundaries or event centers.
Older adults identified event boundaries more frequently overall.

Prolonging pauses at event boundaries did not enhance boundary identification, whereas prolonging pauses at event centers led to boundary identification despite the absence of a major thematic shift, particularly in listeners with poorer hearing.
Hence, aging may change the sensitivity to event boundaries during continuous speech listening, and pause duration can bias event segmentation when thematic cues are absent.
Speech comprehension is critical for communication and social participation.

Much of what we know about it comes from tasks in which listeners repeat or make judgements about short, disconnected sentences (Buss et al., 2019; Fogerty et al., 2021; George et al., 2006; Gifford et al., 2007; Gustafsson & Arlinger, 1994; Herrmann, 2023; Vickery et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Much of what we know about it comes from tasks in which listeners repeat or make judgements about short, disconnected sentences <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Buss et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Fogerty et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">George et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Gifford et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Gustafsson & Arlinger, 1994;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Herrmann, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b151">Vickery et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Such approaches differ from everyday speech perception: speech often unfolds as coherent narratives over tens of seconds to minutes (Bohanek et al., 2009; Hamilton & Huth, 2020; Herrmann & Johnsrude, 2020a; Irsik et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Such approaches differ from everyday speech perception: speech often unfolds as coherent narratives over tens of seconds to minutes <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Bohanek et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Hamilton & Huth, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Herrmann & Johnsrude, 2020a;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">Irsik et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Comprehending this type of speech requires integrating meaning over time to be able to extract the gist, which is not captured well by disconnected sentences.
Event Segmentation Theory (Zacks et al., 2007) offers a framework for assessing how individuals perceive, encode, and recall continuous experiences.
text.formatted: Event Segmentation Theory <ref type="bibr">(Zacks et al., 2007)</ref> offers a framework for assessing how individuals perceive, encode, and recall continuous experiences.

text.text: It posits that experience is organized into discrete, meaningful units, referred to as events (Kurby & Zacks, 2008; Wang et al., 2024; Zacks, 2020; Zacks et al., 2007; Zacks & Swallow, 2007; Zacks & Tversky, 2001).
text.formatted: It posits that experience is organized into discrete, meaningful units, referred to as events <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">(Kurby & Zacks, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b155">Wang et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b160">Zacks, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Zacks et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Zacks & Swallow, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Zacks & Tversky, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: That is, the brain maintains an "event model"a representation of the current situation that helps to predict upcoming information.

Changes in a situation (e.g., moving between rooms) or its features (e.g. time, space, protagonist) are thought to increase prediction errors and trigger model updates that, in turn, yield perceived event boundaries (Zacks, 2020; Zacks et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Changes in a situation (e.g., moving between rooms) or its features (e.g. time, space, protagonist) are thought to increase prediction errors and trigger model updates that, in turn, yield perceived event boundaries <ref type="bibr" target="#b160">(Zacks, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Zacks et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Individuals tend to agree on the placement of boundaries, referred to as "normative boundaries" (Panela et al., 2026; Sasmita & Swallow, 2022; Zacks et al., 2006).
text.formatted: Individuals tend to agree on the placement of boundaries, referred to as "normative boundaries" <ref type="bibr" target="#b107">(Panela et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b129">Sasmita & Swallow, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b163">Zacks et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Segmenting audiovisual or written stories into events aids comprehension and later recall (Boltz, 1992; Lassiter, 1988; Lassiter et al., 1988; Newtson & Engquist, 1976; Schwan & Garsoffky, 2003; Zacks et al., 2006 Zacks et al., , 2007)).
text.formatted: Segmenting audiovisual or written stories into events aids comprehension and later recall <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Boltz, 1992;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">Lassiter, 1988;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">Lassiter et al., 1988;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b102">Newtson & Engquist, 1976;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b133">Schwan & Garsoffky, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b163">Zacks et al., 2006</ref> <ref type="bibr">Zacks et al., , 2007))</ref>.

text.text: Event segmentation thus offers a promising, mechanistically grounded, approach to understanding the comprehension of naturalistic auditory narratives.

Thematic cues, such as changes in time, location, characters, goals, or causal structure, can be potent drivers of event boundaries in narratives (Bamberg & Marchman, 1990; Pettijohn & Radvansky, 2016; Speer & Zacks, 2005; Zwaan et al., 1995; Zwaan & Radvansky, 1998).
text.formatted: Thematic cues, such as changes in time, location, characters, goals, or causal structure, can be potent drivers of event boundaries in narratives <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bamberg & Marchman, 1990;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b111">Pettijohn & Radvansky, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b140">Speer & Zacks, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b167">Zwaan et al., 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b168">Zwaan & Radvansky, 1998)</ref>.

text.text: For auditory narratives, however, the auditory signal itself may also carry information that could scaffold segmentation.
Prosody marks structure in narratives through coordinated patterns of pitch, duration, and timing (Brugos et al., 2018; Féry, 2016; Frazier et al., 2006).
text.formatted: Prosody marks structure in narratives through coordinated patterns of pitch, duration, and timing <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Brugos et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Féry, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Frazier et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Among these cues, sentence-level silent pauses are especially relevant for higher-level grouping because they punctuate larger units and are salient to listeners (Blau, 1990; Jacobs, 1988).
text.formatted: Among these cues, sentence-level silent pauses are especially relevant for higher-level grouping because they punctuate larger units and are salient to listeners <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Blau, 1990;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Jacobs, 1988)</ref>.

text.text: In news broadcasts, longer pauses mark topic shifts (Shriberg et al., 2000; Tür et al., 2001), but whether this extends to other narratives is unclear.
text.formatted: In news broadcasts, longer pauses mark topic shifts <ref type="bibr" target="#b135">(Shriberg et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b147">Tür et al., 2001)</ref>, but whether this extends to other narratives is unclear.

text.text: Moreover, topics can span multiple events, leaving unanswered whether speakers use longer pauses to mark event boundaries in non-news speech.

This question is also relevant for modern text-to-speech systems, which are increasingly used in research and daily life (Ammari et al., 2019; Bentley et al., 2018; Buteau & Lee, 2021; Herrmann, 2023 Herrmann, , 2025c)), and may already be using, or could benefit from, human-like pausing at event boundaries.
text.formatted: This question is also relevant for modern text-to-speech systems, which are increasingly used in research and daily life <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Ammari et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Bentley et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Buteau & Lee, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Herrmann, 2023</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Herrmann, , 2025c))</ref>, and may already be using, or could benefit from, human-like pausing at event boundaries.

text.text: Even if people and modern text-to-speech systems produce lengthened pause durations to mark event boundaries in speech, it does not necessarily follow that individuals use such cues to identify meaningful units during listening.
The interplay of acoustic and thematic cues in speech comprehension is also unclear.

Most work on how people segment ongoing input into events has been conducted using visual (reading, silent films) (e.g., Bailey et al., 2017; Feller et al., 2019; Newberry et al., 2021; Swets & Kurby, 2016) or audiovisual (movie) materials (e.g., Boltz, 1992; Sasmita & Swallow, 2022; Schwan & Garsoffky, 2004; Zacks et al., 2009).

text.text: These materials, however, are unfit for studying acoustic cues in event segmentation, since listeners cannot revisit the input or rely on visual cues and have to segment a transient signal structured largely by prosody.

text.text: Whether event segmentation in auditory speech and the use of acoustic cues, such as pauses, differ between older and younger adults is unclear.
The present study investigates how thematic and pause-duration cues affect the identification of event boundaries during naturalistic speech listening in younger and older adults.

After obtaining normative thematic event boundaries via an LLM approach (Michelmann et al., 2025; Panela et al., 2025), we first examine whether human speakers lengthen pauses at these boundaries and whether modern text-tospeech systems mirror these timing cues (Experiment 1).

text.text: We then investigate whether pause lengthening at thematic boundaries shapes listeners' perception and how this interacts with age, hearing, and cognitive abilities (Experiment 2).
Together, the current study provides a comprehensive account of how thematic and pauseduration information shapes event segmentation during speech listening in younger and older adults.
Experiment 1 investigated whether pause lengthening marks event boundaries in human and in AI-synthesized speech.
We obtained human audio recordings and transcripts, generated AI-voice audio from the same transcripts, and used a LLM to identify event boundaries in those transcripts.
We then analyzed the audio recordings for pause lengthening at those boundaries.

We analyzed 200 existing auditory stories in American English: 100 audiobooks (stories read aloud) and 100 monologues (podcast stories told to an audience).

text.text: The output of each pipeline contained onset and offset times for each word of a story.
Around 10% of the stories where background sound effects overlapped with the speech and impeded estimating pause durations were excluded from the sample. (audiobooks: 10 files; monologues: 9 files).
We calculated pause durations at event boundaries and at event centers, the latter reflecting the sentence transition approximately midway between two boundaries.
Because event boundaries always fell between sentences, event centers were also placed between sentences to allow comparison.
Pause duration was defined as the interval between the offset of a sentence's last word and the onset of the next sentence's first word.

For each story, voice (the original human voice and the three AI voices), and each of the three different forced alignment approaches, we computed the median pause duration across boundaries and across centers.

Thirty-six younger adults (median age: 21 years, age range: 19-35 years; 3 male, 28 female, 3 non-binary, 1 agender, 1 non-gender conforming) and thirty-six older adults (median age: 69.5 years, age range: 56-79 years; 18 male, 18 female) participated in the study.
We performed a post hoc sensitivity analysis to ensure the sample size had sufficient power (see Supplement 3).
Participants were native English speakers or had learned English before the age of 5 (for participants' ethnicity and second language abilities see Supplement 4).
They reported having normal hearing and no neurological diseases.
One person reported autism, but this did not affect their participation.
None of the participants wore or had been prescribed hearing aids.
Pure-tone audiometry was conducted at 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, and 8 kHz using a Maico M28 audiometer.

text.text: Instructions before the practice run were as follows:

You will listen to the same story the second time.
Please now identify the largest meaningful event units.

Agreement index.

Consistency of boundary placement across participants is commonly measured with the agreement index, or inter-subject correlation (Panela et al., 2025; Sasmita & Swallow, 2022; Newtson, 1973; Newtson et al., 1977; Newtson & Engquist, 1976; Zacks et al., 2006; Zacks & Tversky, 2001), which quantifies how closely an individual's segmentation aligns with that of the group (Sasmita & Swallow, 2022; Zacks et al., 2006).

text.text: For each participant and story/pause-condition, button presses were coded as 1s in an otherwise zero time series sampled at 50 Hz (0.02 s time steps).
Time series were convolved with a Gaussian kernel (SD = 2 s) (Huff et al., 2017 (Huff et al., , 2018;; Newberry et al., 2021) to account for variability in response timing across participants.

text.text: Each participant's time series was then correlated (Pearson's r) with the average time series of all other participants who heard the same story in the same pause condition, with higher values indicating greater agreement.
A LMM was fit using the agreement indices as the dependent measure, Pause Condition, Age Group and their interaction as fixed effects, and random intercepts for participant and story.

The agreement index summarizes segmentation patterns across an entire story (Sasmita & Swallow, 2022; Zacks et al., 2006), but does not show when participants responded relative to specific points in the story.

text.text: We therefore computed time courses of button presses around event boundaries and event centers (hereafter, reference points).

Analogous to event-related potentials in EEG (Luck, 2014), event-related pupil responses (Mathôt et al., 2018), and, most closely, peri-stimulus histograms of neural spiking (Gerstein & Kiang, 1960), this approach averages responses time-locked to recurring reference points, here button presses.
text.formatted: Analogous to event-related potentials in EEG <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">(Luck, 2014)</ref>, event-related pupil responses <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">(Mathôt et al., 2018)</ref>, and, most closely, peri-stimulus histograms of neural spiking <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Gerstein & Kiang, 1960)</ref>, this approach averages responses time-locked to recurring reference points, here button presses.

text.text: For each participant and pause condition, button presses were placed on a timeline, where t = 0 was the reference point, and the full timeline (epoch) spanned -10 to +10 s around this point, allowing us to characterize responses over a broad temporal interval.
A 2-s window was moved across this epoch in 0.05-s steps.

At each step, the number of button presses within the window was divided by the number of reference points (event boundaries or event centers) in the story, providing a proportion of button presses in this window (as compared to the whole story).
Taken together at all steps, proportions of button presses (response rates) result in time courses, which provide a measure of how responding changed around boundaries and centers.
The 2-s window smooths over small differences in response timing.
Because each reference point is a pause, t = 0 can be placed at either edge of it: the offset of the preceding sentence or the onset of the following sentence.
We computed time courses for both.
Offset-locked time courses test whether responses follow the end of the preceding event, whereas onset-locked time courses test whether they follow the beginning of the next event.
This distinction is important for our manipulated conditions, where the added 1 s of silence separates the two edges of the pause further.
For statistical analysis, response rates were averaged within a pre-reference window (-3 to -1 s) and a post-reference window (+1 to +3 s), chosen based on the evolution of the time courses.

First, to test whether responding increased more after event boundaries than after event centers in speech without pause manipulations, response rates in the Original condition were analyzed with an LMM, including the factors of Reference Point (event boundary, event center), Time Window (pre, post), Age Group and their interactions as fixed effects and a random intercept for participant.

Second, to test the pause manipulation, we computed the change in response rate from the pre-to the post-reference window (post-minus-pre = response_rate(+1 to +3) -response_rate(-3 to -1)) for each participant, pause condition, and reference point.
This "baseline corrected" (Luck, 2014) response rate accounts for individual and group differences and biases in overall responses.

The first model isolated the influence of thematic shifts, using the baseline-corrected response rate at event boundaries in the 'Original' pause condition as the dependent variable.
The second model isolated the influence of prolonged pauses, using the baseline-corrected response rate at event centers in the 'Event-Center Pause' condition as the dependent variable.

text.text: We examined how pause duration and thematic shifts shape event segmentation in spoken stories.
Experiment 1 shows that humans and modern AI voices produce longer pauses at event boundaries compared to event centers.
Experiment 2 focused on whether pause durations are used by younger and older listeners to identify event boundaries.
Older adults were more likely to identify event boundaries.

Critically, we show for both age groups that pause lengthening does not contribute to event segmentation when a thematic story shift is present (i.e., at event boundaries), but that pause lengthening can lead to event segmentation in the absence of a thematic story shift (i.e., at event centers), especially for individuals with lowered hearing abilities.
Our findings highlight the interplay between thematic and acoustic cues in producing and perceiving event boundaries. center for the Event-Center Pause condition as a function of PTA.

The results of Experiment 1 show that human speakers produce longer pauses at event boundaries compared to event centers.

This aligns with work showing that prosodic cues are crucial in signaling sentence boundaries in speech (Brugos et al., 2018; Frazier et al., 2006; Wagner & Watson, 2010), and topic shifts in news speech (Pfeiffer, 2001; Shriberg et al., 2000; Tür et al., 2001).

text.text: Pause lengthening by speakers could potentially reflect different functions: real-time event processing by the speaker, a tendency for the speaker to aid event segmentation for the listener, or both.
Disentangling these potential functions requires further research.
Experiment 1 also demonstrated that modern AI-based text-to-speech synthesizers capture this trend as well.
That is, we found that a recent-generation AI voice -OpenAI's "Alloy" -produced longer pauses at event boundaries than at event centers.
Older generations of text-to-speech models (e.g.
Google's "Casual" or "Studio" voices) tended to exhibit a more uniform distribution of pause durations.

Perhaps the results may be expected, given that the speech input for model training may likely be based on audiobooks and podcasts, leading advanced models to capture human speech-production patterns.

The results of Experiment 2 show that listeners consistently identify event boundaries during continuous story listening, in agreement with previous work (Kumar et al., 2023; Michelmann et al., 2021; Zacks et al., 2009).

text.text: For our experimental manipulation and main analysis, we used event boundaries derived from LLMs (Michelmann et al., 2025; Panela et al., 2025), and the results confirm that humans identify event boundaries that were also identified by the LLM (Figure 6; supplementary Figure S2).

text.text: Experiment 2 further suggests that participants identified event boundaries based on information at the end of an event rather than waiting for a new event to begin (Figure 5).
text.formatted: Experiment 2 further suggests that participants identified event boundaries based on information at the end of an event rather than waiting for a new event to begin (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_6">5</ref>).

text.text: That is, in time courses locked to event onsets, responses in the Original condition peaked about 1 second after event onset, but when pauses at event boundaries were lengthened, the response peak was located at event onset.
Little to no information about the new event was available at this time.
Had the listeners waited for the new event to unfold, response latencies relative to event onset should not have differed between conditions.
Consistent with this, offset-locked responses peaked at similar times in both conditions (Figure 5).
text.formatted: Consistent with this, offset-locked responses peaked at similar times in both conditions (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_6">5</ref>).

text.text: Listeners thus appear to detect event boundaries from event endings rather than beginnings.

This finding may contradict the framework proposed by the Event Segmentation Theory, which posits that event boundary perception is driven by prediction error elicited through the attempted integration of novel information into the current event model (Kurby & Zacks, 2008; Zacks et al., 2007; Zacks & Swallow, 2007).

text.text: Our current results suggest that participants anticipate the near completion of an event rather than responding to a prediction error.

Recent research has indicated that event segmentation may also be driven by prediction uncertainty (Franklin et al., 2020; Nguyen et al., 2024) such that event boundaries are perceived when the strength of predictions derived through the current event model reduces.

text.text: Our data could thus reflect participants anticipating the impeding end to an event through the decrease in prediction strength.

Responses after event ends could also be triggered by silence; however, silence alone is unlikely to drive boundary identification: responses at prolonged pauses were still significantly larger at boundaries than at event centers, indicating a role for thematic shifts.
Older adults indicated the presence of an event boundary more frequently than younger adults, although the agreement with the event boundary placement did not differ between age groups (Figure 4B).

text.text: Findings about age-related changes in event segmentation are mixed.
Research using audiovisual depictions of everyday activities suggests lower segmentation agreement and poorer recognition of event structure in older adults (Kurby & Zacks, 2011; Zacks et al., 2006).
text.formatted: Research using audiovisual depictions of everyday activities suggests lower segmentation agreement and poorer recognition of event structure in older adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">(Kurby & Zacks, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b163">Zacks et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: These declines have been attributed to age-related decreases in attention, working memory capacity, or processing speed (Kurby & Zacks, 2011; Noh & Stine-Morrow, 2009; Smith et al., 2020; Zacks et al., 2006).
text.formatted: These declines have been attributed to age-related decreases in attention, working memory capacity, or processing speed <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">(Kurby & Zacks, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b104">Noh & Stine-Morrow, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b136">Smith et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b163">Zacks et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Nevertheless, other studies align more with the current findings, suggesting that event perception in movies (Kurby & Zacks, 2018) and written texts (Davis & Campbell, 2023; Radvansky et al., 2003; Radvansky & Copeland, 2001) is preserved with age, especially when using well-structured stimuli.

text.text: Older adults have sometimes demonstrated segmenting written and picture stories into fine-grained events (Magliano et al., 2012), although this is not always the case (Kurby & Zacks, 2011).

text.text: Finer segmentation could imply that older adults have a lower threshold or shifted criterion for what counts as a meaningful thematic shift, such that they identify an event boundary even for less salient thematic shifts.
This would be consistent with older adults' somewhat higher, though still low, rate of responses at event centers.
Finer segmentation has been attributed to memory decline in older people (Braver & West, 2011), but neither memory span nor fluid intelligence predicted event segmentation in our study.

text.text: The current results suggest that thematic shifts and acoustic cues interact when shaping event segmentation.

Our observations and many previous studies have shown that thematic changes correlate with perceived event boundaries (Magliano et al., 2012; Zacks, 2020; Zacks et al., 2007 Zacks et al., , 2009;; Zwaan et al., 1995; Zwaan & Radvansky, 1998), although this has been much less investigated for speech listening (Kumar et al., 2023; Michelmann et al., 2021; see also Supplementary Materials).
text.formatted: Our observations and many previous studies have shown that thematic changes correlate with perceived event boundaries <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">(Magliano et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b160">Zacks, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Zacks et al., 2007</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b161">Zacks et al., , 2009;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b167">Zwaan et al., 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b168">Zwaan & Radvansky, 1998)</ref>, although this has been much less investigated for speech listening <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">(Kumar et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b96">Michelmann et al., 2021</ref>; see also Supplementary Materials).

text.text: Thematic cues indicating event transitions provide a strong contribution to narrative structure organization (Bamberg & Marchman, 1990; Feller et al., 2019; Tür et al., 2001) and have been shown to increase the probability of event boundary responses (Davis & Campbell, 2023; Ezzyat & Davachi, 2011).

text.text: Our data suggest that pause lengthening at event boundaries, however, did not further increase the probability for listeners to identify boundaries.
Therefore, longer pauses may not provide additional information when a clear thematic shift is present in the narrative.

In contrast to event boundaries, prolonging pauses at event centersthat is, time points in the middle between two major narrative shiftsincreased the probability of an event segmentation response for listeners.
The data thus indicate that in the absence of a thematic shift, pause durations can bias listeners into perceiving a boundary.

Interestingly, we observed that the bias of perceiving an event boundary due to pause lengthening in the absence of a thematic shift (i.e., at the event center) was greater in people with greater hearing loss as indicated by the pure-tone average threshold.

Hearing loss can lead to perceptual and neural hypersensitivity to sound (Baguley, 2003; Herrmann & Butler, 2021; Irsik et al., 2021; Tyler et al., 2014) that may particularly be expressed for sounds after a longer pause.
text.formatted: Hearing loss can lead to perceptual and neural hypersensitivity to sound <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Baguley, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Herrmann & Butler, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Irsik et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b148">Tyler et al., 2014</ref>) that may particularly be expressed for sounds after a longer pause.

text.text: Possibly, cochlear and neural changes associated with hearing loss result in greater sensitivity to acoustic cues that are then interpreted as a sign of an event in a story ending and a new event starting in the absence of a thematic shift.
The scope of the study, however, limits this result to non-clinical hearing loss, given the sample characteristics (self-reported normal hearing, no hearing aids, and mild audiometric thresholds).
This connection, therefore, needs to be further investigated in detail in clinical settings.

We also need to remark that Experiment 2 used a single AI voice and only three stories, requiring further work to confirm generalizability to human speech (despite high naturalness of AI voices) and a broader range of narratives.
We examined how speakers mark event boundaries in spoken stories and how listeners use pauses and thematic shifts to perceive them.
Both human and AI speakers lengthened pauses at event boundaries.
Listeners, however, relied primarily on thematic content and used pauses mainly when thematic cues were absent, particularly listeners with poorer hearing.
Older adults identified event boundaries more often than younger adults.

Together, these findings extend event segmentation research to the auditory domain and show that the way listeners organize continuous speech depends on the interplay of narrative content, acoustic cues, age, and hearing.
